models_evaluated: prototype-based XAI model for gestational age estimation

links.outcome: Clinician gestational age error with versus without AI predictions and explanations
links.effect: Model predictions reduced clinician MAE from 23.5 to 15.7 days; explanations gave a further non-significant reduction to 14.3 days; effect of explanations varied across participants.
links.quote: Model predictions reduced clinician mean absolute error (MAE) from 23.5 to 15.7 days, and explanations had a further non-significant reduction to 14.3 days.

links.outcome: Effect of AI explanations on clinician trust, reliance, confidence, and performance
links.effect: Explanations increased participant confidence but had no significant effect on trust or reliance; some participants performed worse with explanations than without.
links.quote: Additionally, although explanations increased participant confidence, they had no significant effect on trust or reliance on the model.

models_evaluated: prototype-based XAI model for image-based gestational age estimation

links.effect: Model predictions reduced MAE from 23.5 to 15.7 days; explanations further, non-significantly, to 14.3 days.
links.quote: Model predictions reduced clinician mean absolute error (MAE) from 23.5 to 15.7 days, and explanations had a further non-significant reduction to 14.3 days.

links.effect: Explanations non-significantly reduced MAE to 14.3 days, but effects varied and some participants performed worse.
links.quote: However, the impact of explanations varied across participants, with some performing worse with explanations than without.

links.effect: Human testing found clinician variability: some worse with explanations; confidence increased but no significant trust or reliance effect.
links.quote: These counterintuitive results highlight potential pitfalls in deploying XAI, emphasising the need for human studies to capture clinician variability.
